sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title (Lionnet 2019, WCCFL 36) was already held by the project with a native text and was read in full; written under It is a prosody paper about tone/downstep and foot-colon structure in Paicî, not about word stress; it never attributes stress or accent to Paicî and confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding (its deciding source, Lionnet 2022 PDA, is the fuller peer-reviewed sequel by the same author and remains the better citation). No new stress statement found; nothing to acquire. Leads seen only as bibliographic records in the 2019/2022 reference lists, not downloaded: Rivierre 1974 'Tons et segments du discours en paicî' (BSL 69:1, 325-340) and Rivierre 1978 'Accents, tons et inversion tonale en Nouvelle-Calédonie' (BSL 73:1) — the latter is the historical-accent source (Xârâcùù initial accent vs. Paicî downstep) that the catalog already summarises via Lionnet 2022 §6.4; medium priority if a first-hand French statement of the pre-tonogenesis accent is ever wanted. web look-ups were unnecessary for the single item.

new_statements.quote: Paicî is a tonal language. The tone-bearing unit is the mora. ... Downstep is illustrated in (6): while L-toned words of one to three morae are realized with a level L tone throughout (6a), words of four morae and above undergo a register drop after the second mora (6b). ... As seen, downstep can only occur if there are two adjacent L-toned bimoraic feet, i.e. if there are at least four morae.
new_statements.citation: Lionnet, Florian. 2019. The colon as a separate prosodic category: tonal evidence from Paicî (Oceanic, New Caledonia). Proceedings of WCCFL 36, 250-259. Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
new_statements.reading: Not a stress statement: the paper's only first-hand word-prosodic claim for Paicî is that it is a two-tone, mora-counting language whose L-toned words of four or more morae get a downstep after the initial bimoraic foot (left-edge foot/colon parsing visible only through tone). No word stress or accent is posited; the author frames the metrical structure as tonal, not stress-based. This is the earlier, shorter version of the same author's 2022 PDA article that the catalog already uses, and it agrees with the catalog's 'tonal' coding.

tone_statements.quote: Le paicî est une langue tonale qui comprend trois tons : haut, bas et moyen. Ces tons permettent de distinguer deux mots dont le signifiant est le même mais qui ne désignent pas le même signifié, comme dans les exemples suivants : u (ton haut) "genie" vs u (ton moyen) "vent" pwâ (ton haut) "bouche" vs pwâ (ton moyen) "tortue" La notation des tons ne semble pas essentielle dans l’écriture courante, bien qu’elle soit utile pour les non locuteurs afin de préciser la bonne prononciation des termes.
tone_statements.translation: Paicî is a tone language with three tones: high, low and mid. These tones distinguish two words with the same segmental form but different meanings, as in: u (high tone) 'spirit' vs u (mid tone) 'wind'; pwâ (high tone) 'mouth' vs pwâ (mid tone) 'turtle'. Tone marking does not seem essential in everyday writing, although it is useful for non-speakers to indicate the correct pronunciation.

sources.note: Nothing about word stress in Paicî: the word 'stress' occurs only for other languages (Hungarian, Passamaquoddy, Iquito etc.) and in the framing claim that metrical structure is relevant 'in domains other than stress, e.g. tone'. sources.citation: Lionnet, Florian. 2025. Accent and tone: The double origin of the Paicî prosodic system. Diachronica 42(3-4): 406-427.
sources.note: Paicî 'seems to possess two integrated prosodic subsystems: a purely tonal H vs. L contrast, and a typologically unusual downstep with accentual properties'; building on Rivierre (1978), comparison with Xârâcùù (accent marked by a similar downstep) shows the H/L contrast emerged through tonogenesis in an already accentual language, the former accentual downstep being reinterpreted as tonal. Agrees with the statement listed here (H, L + downstep).

In Anne-Laure Dotte, Stéphanie Geneix-Rabault & Suzie Bearune (eds.), Uane nore nodei lanengoc – Penser les langues – Thinking about languages: Actes de la 11e Conférence de Linguistique Océanienne (COOL 11), 47-68. sources.note: Analysis of the role of prosodic structure in the Paicî tone system, continuing Rivierre 1974, with Rivierre's data plus new field data (Lionnet et al. 2020); the Paicî tone system gives evidence for an abstract prosodic structure independent of morphosyntax and for the 'colon' (two metrical feet) in the prosodic hierarchy. Consistent with the on-file H/L + metrically placed downstep account.
